summary_html: CPS **accepts** a report for **investigation/assessment**. CAPTA sets the floor for investigation procedures; CFSR evaluates timeliness, safety, and decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — investigation standards tied to funding  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — timeliness & response conformity indicators

primary_citations.citation_text: Montana - Title 41, Chapter 3 (Child Abuse and Neglect – mandatory reporting and protective services)

regulations_applicable.title: Department 37 - PUBLIC HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Termination was affirmed; a youth-in-need-of-care adjudication is not a prerequisite to temporary investigative authority under § 41-3-433 or to a court-ordered treatment plan under § 41-3-443(1) where the parents admit or stipulate to the allegations.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Montana authority on the temporary-investigative-authority track for accepting a case for formal investigation.
key_cases.quote: a YINC adjudication is not always required for TIA and court-approved treatment plans

key_cases.holding: The district court did not err in dismissing the abuse and neglect proceeding after the child was returned to the custodial mother in South Carolina; the court properly exercised emergency jurisdiction, which ended with the return, and any procedural irregularities did not prejudice the father, whose parental rights remained intact.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Montana authority on the depth of investigation owed to a non-custodial parent before the child is placed with him.
key_cases.quote: This further investigation when objective concerns regarding the safety of the non-custodial parent are raised during the initial investigation is required.

key_cases.holding: An interlocutory order granting temporary investigative authority and protective services is not appealable under Rule 1, M.R.App.P.; review must be sought by certiorari, habeas corpus or supervisory control, although the Court suspended the rules and reached the merits here because the parties had relied on a contrary prior statement.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Montana template for what an acceptance-for-investigation petition must contain and how the court tests it.
key_cases.quote: We hold, therefore, that an interlocutory order granting temporary investigative authority and protective services is not appealable under Rule 1, M.R.App.P.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: A social worker and a police officer who coerced entry into a family home to investigate an anonymous abuse report, without a warrant, consent or exigency, and who had a child's clothing removed for a visual inspection, were not entitled to qualified immunity; the administrative-search doctrine does not exempt child-protection home entries.
key_cases.relevance: It defines the constitutional limits on how a Montana caseworker may conduct the home visit that an accepted report triggers.
key_cases.quote: Under White, appellants' claim, that “a search warrant is not required for home investigatory visits by social workers,” is simply not the law.

key_cases.holding: Termination of an out-of-state, non-custodial father's rights was reversed for ineffective assistance of counsel and the case rewound to the adjudication stage: on removal from the custodial parent the Department must first consider placement with the non-custodial parent after a preliminary assessment, and may expand the investigation or impose an ICPC or treatment plan only where objective, demonstrable circumstances show an imminent safety risk.
key_cases.relevance: It is the source of Montana's rule on how deeply the Department must assess a non-custodial parent once a report is accepted for investigation, and In re D.H. does nothing but apply its paragraph 29.
key_cases.quote: Upon removal of a child from a custodial parent, the Department must first consider placement of the child with the non-custodial parent.
